title: How to Start Family Worship in Five Minutes
excerpt: Family worship is not a production. It is a few honest minutes around a table, repeated until it becomes the air your children breathe.
body:
Most parents who want family worship never start it, and the reason is almost always the same. They are waiting to feel ready, to find the right book, to have a house calm enough to pull it off. That day does not come. Your children grow up in the house you actually have, not the one you keep meaning to build. So start small enough that you cannot fail.

## Why five minutes is the right size

Family worship has a long history, and almost none of it looks like a polished thirty-minute lesson. The Puritans called it the duty of the household, and what they meant was simple: a father or mother gathering the people under their roof to read a little Scripture, pray, and sing. Deuteronomy 6 tells parents to talk of God's commands "when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise." That is not a curriculum. It is a rhythm woven through an ordinary day.

Five minutes works because you will actually do it. A practice you keep beats a practice you admire. I have abandoned more ambitious plans than I can count. The nights we simply read three verses and prayed are the nights my sons remember.

## The three movements

Keep it to three things. Read, talk, pray.

**Read.** Pick one short passage. A psalm, a few verses from the Gospel you are walking through, a proverb. Read it aloud. Do not explain everything. Let the words sit.

**Talk.** Ask one question. Not a quiz. "What do you think God is like in this verse?" or "What is hard to believe here?" Let a child's strange answer stand without correcting it into the ground. You are training them to bring their real thoughts to Scripture, not to perform the right ones.

**Pray.** Short prayers, out loud, by name. Pray for the math test. Pray for the grandmother in the hospital. Let the children pray too, even when it is one mumbled sentence. They are learning that God is spoken to, not just spoken about.

## Pick a time you already own

Do not invent a new slot in the day. Attach worship to something that already happens. Dinner is the obvious one, because everyone is already sitting and trapped. Bedtime works for younger children. Breakfast works if your mornings are not a war.

The anchor matters more than the hour. If you try to do it whenever there is a gap, there will never be a gap. Choose the meal or the moment, and let the consistency carry you on the nights you have nothing left.

## Expect it to go badly

It will. Someone will be in a mood. A toddler will throw a fork during the prayer. A teenager will sigh like you have asked for blood. You will feel like a fraud reading about grace through clenched teeth.

Keep going anyway. The point was never a perfect five minutes. The point is that your children grow up knowing this family stops, opens the Bible, and talks to God. That memory forms slowly, under the surface, through a hundred mediocre evenings. You are not staging a moment. You are laying down a riverbed.

Resist the urge to lecture. The temptation in family worship is to turn five minutes into a sermon because you finally have a captive audience. Do not. Read, ask, pray, release them. A short practice they do not dread will outlast a long one they endure.

## This week

Pick the meal. Tonight or tomorrow, before anyone leaves the table, read one psalm, ask one question, and pray for one thing by name. Do not announce a new program. Just do it, and do it again the next night. Give it two weeks before you judge whether it is working. By then it will have started to belong to you.

If you want a structure to lean on, the family devotions and catechism resources at /family/devotions and /family/catechism give you the words for the nights you have none. But the words are not the point. The showing up is the point. Start with five minutes you can keep.

title: How to Have the Screen Conversation by Age
excerpt: The screen conversation is not one talk. It is a different conversation at five, at ten, at fifteen, and the version that works changes as fast as the child does.
body:
Parents tend to treat screens as a single fight to be won once, usually by setting a rule and defending it. But the child at five who needs a hand pulled off the tablet is not the child at fifteen who carries the entire internet in a back pocket. The conversation has to grow up alongside the kid, or it stops being a conversation and becomes a war of attrition you will eventually lose.

I did not get this right. I set rules I could not hold and gave speeches my sons stopped hearing. What follows is what I wish I had understood earlier, sorted by the age you are actually parenting.

## The early years: you are the limit

From roughly three to eight, the child has no internal brake, and you should not pretend otherwise. This is the season of external structure. Screens live in shared spaces. Time is finite and predictable. You decide, and you do not negotiate it like a hostage situation.

The conversation here is mostly about naming. "Screens are fun, and they are designed to be hard to stop. That is why we turn it off, and it is also why turning it off feels hard." You are teaching a young child that the pull they feel is real, has a cause, and can be resisted. You are also modeling it. A parent scrolling through dinner has already lost the argument before it starts. I have lost it that way more than once.

## The middle years: the why begins

From roughly nine to twelve, the child starts asking why, and "because I said so" curdles into resentment if it is your only answer. This is the season to give reasons and let them be questioned.

Talk about what the device is doing to attention, to sleep, to the way comparison creeps in. Be honest that companies build these things to be hard to put down and that this is not an accident. Twelve-year-olds can handle the truth that they are being engineered, and they tend to respect a parent who tells it to them straight.

This is also the age to start the conversation about what they will see that they did not go looking for. They will encounter cruelty and pornography and despair on the other side of a screen, often before they are ready. Tell them now: when you see something that scares or shames you, come to me, and I will not be angry. The point is to be the safe place before they need one.

## The teen years: from control to coaching

By thirteen and up, the phone is usually in their hand, and the question shifts. You are no longer the wall. You are the coach. A teenager who is controlled but never taught becomes an adult with no internal compass and a sudden, total freedom. That is the worst possible outcome, and rigid control quietly produces it.

The conversation here is about formation, not just restriction. Talk about who they are becoming in the hours they scroll. Ask what an account makes them feel, and whether they want to feel that. Set limits still, but set them with them, out loud, with reasons they can argue. Galatians warns against being mastered by anything. Frame it that way: not "the phone is bad," but "is anything mastering you, and how would you know?"

## What stays constant

Across every age, three things hold.

First, your own phone is the loudest sermon you preach. Children calibrate to what you do, not what you say.

Second, the goal is self-governance, not lifelong surveillance. Every year you should be transferring a little more of the controls from your hands to theirs, on purpose, with conversation.

Third, keep the door open. The worst screen damage happens in secret, to children who believe a parent will explode. Be the harbor, even when what they confess makes your stomach drop.

## This week

Name the age you are actually parenting and have the version of the conversation that fits it. For a young child, narrate one turn-off out loud. For a middle child, give one real reason behind one real rule. For a teenager, ask one genuine question about how a screen makes them feel, and listen without fixing it. Then look at your own usage for a single day and let what you find correct you before you correct anyone else.

title: How to Discipline in a Way That Reaches the Heart
excerpt: Most discipline manages behavior and never touches the heart underneath it. Reaching the heart is slower, harder, and the only thing that lasts.
body:
It is possible to raise a child who obeys and resents you, who keeps the rules and learns nothing but how to avoid getting caught. Discipline that only manages behavior produces exactly that. The Bible aims somewhere deeper. "Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life," says Proverbs. The behavior is a symptom. The heart is the thing.

This does not mean rules are wrong or consequences are cruel. It means consequences are the beginning of the conversation, not the whole of it. Here is how to discipline so that you are forming a person, not just suppressing a problem.

## Get yourself under control first

Most bad discipline is a parent's anger wearing the costume of correction. We tell ourselves we are teaching a lesson when we are actually discharging frustration. The child can tell the difference, and what they learn is that power flows to whoever is loudest.

Before you correct, get your own heart in hand. James is blunt: "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God." If you are too hot to be just, say so and step away. "I am too angry to talk about this right now. We will deal with it in ten minutes." That sentence teaches more about self-control than any lecture you could deliver in the heat.

## Aim for the why, not just the what

When you correct, do not stop at the behavior. Get underneath it. A child who hit a sibling did something. But why? Fear of losing? A sense of being treated unfairly? A habit of grabbing what they want? The behavior is the same; the heart driving it is not, and the correction should follow the heart.

Ask real questions. "What were you wanting when you did that?" "What were you afraid would happen?" You are not excusing the act. You are helping a child see themselves, which is the only path to actually changing. A child who only knows the rule will break it the moment no one is watching. A child who understands their own heart has somewhere to grow from.

## Let consequences be honest, not theatrical

Consequences should fit the offense and connect to it. A child who makes a mess cleans it up. A child who abuses a privilege loses it for a while. The consequence teaches because it tells the truth about how the world works, not because it makes the child suffer enough to satisfy you.

Resist consequences that are really just punishment for embarrassing you. And resist the opposite error of letting everything slide because confrontation is exhausting. A child needs to bump into firm and predictable limits to feel safe. Inconsistency is its own kind of cruelty, because the child can never tell where the ground is.

## Always reconnect afterward

Discipline that ends in distance has missed the point. The goal of correction in Scripture is restoration, not exile. The father in the story of the prodigal does not make the son earn his way back through a probation period. He runs.

So after the consequence, after the hard conversation, come back. Hold the child. Tell them you love them and that nothing they did changed that. This is where the heart gets reached, in the moment they discover that being corrected did not cost them your love. That is the whole gospel in a single bedtime: you are not what you did, you are still mine, come here.

This is also where most of us fail, myself included. We are good at the consequence and terrible at the reconciliation, because we are still nursing the offense. Reconnecting while you are still a little angry is the discipline behind the discipline.

## This week

The next time you have to correct a child, do three things in order. Get your own anger in hand before you say a word, even if it means waiting. Ask one question about what was going on in their heart, not just what their hands did. And when it is over, reconnect on purpose, out loud, so they leave the moment certain they are still loved. Watch what changes when correction ends in an embrace instead of a slammed door.

title: How to Talk to Your Kids About Sex
excerpt: The sex talk is not a single dreaded event but a long, ordinary conversation. If you do not have it, the culture and the search bar will have it for you.
body:
Many Christian parents are still waiting for the right moment to have the talk, and the right moment passed years ago. By the time you sit your child down for the formal version, they have already absorbed a hundred messages from screens, friends, and a culture that is not shy. The question was never whether your child would learn about sex. The question is whether you would be one of the voices they learned from, or the one voice that stayed silent.

Silence is not neutrality. Silence teaches that this is shameful, that the parents cannot be asked, that the answers must be found elsewhere. That is the opposite of what you want.

## Make it a conversation, not an event

The single most freeing shift is this: it is not one talk. It is dozens of small, low-stakes conversations spread across years. A toddler asks where babies come from and you give a true, simple answer. A seven-year-old hears a word on the bus and you explain it plainly. A twelve-year-old's body starts changing and you are already someone they can ask.

This takes the pressure off the dreaded sit-down. You are not delivering one terrifying lecture. You are being askable, over and over, until your child knows that no question will shock you out of the room.

## Use real words and a calm face

Use the actual names for body parts from the beginning. Coded language teaches shame before you have said anything about it. A parent who can name the body without flinching tells a child that this is good, made by God, and not dirty.

Genesis says God made us male and female and called it very good. The Song of Songs puts an entire book of married desire in the canon without apology. The Christian story does not treat the body as an embarrassment. Your face should match that theology. When your child asks something, the goal is a calm, unstartled answer, even when your insides are doing something else.

## Give the meaning, not just the mechanics

The culture is happy to teach your children the mechanics. What it will not teach them is what sex is for. This is the part only you can give.

Tell them sex is not shameful and not casual. It is a covenant act, a sign of a promise, the kind of self-giving that belongs inside a love that has bound itself for life. Frame it as something honored, not something forbidden. "Wait" lands very differently when it means "this is too good to spend cheaply" than when it means "this is dirty and dangerous." One produces freedom. The other produces shame, and shame does not actually keep anyone pure. It just keeps them quiet.

## Talk about what they will actually encounter

Name the things they will meet, before they meet them. They will see pornography, probably younger than you would guess and probably by accident first. Tell them now what it is and why it lies about sex, that it shows bodies without persons and pleasure without covenant. Tell them that if they stumble into it, or go looking and feel ashamed, they can come to you, and you will not detonate.

This is the hardest promise to keep and the most important. The child who believes a parent will react with horror is the child who hides everything. Be the one they can tell. Your steadiness when they confess is worth more than any rule you could enforce.

## Stay ahead of the changing body

Do not let puberty arrive as a surprise that nobody warned them about. A child whose body starts changing without a single honest word from a parent assumes something is wrong with them, or that this too belongs in the category of the unspeakable. Talk about it before it happens, plainly and matter-of-factly, so that when it comes they meet it as something expected and good rather than alarming and shameful. The body God designed is doing exactly what it was made to do, and your child should hear that from you first.

## Match your words to their age

What you say at five is not what you say at fifteen, and trying to deliver the whole truth at once either overwhelms a small child or arrives years too late for an older one. Give a little child a simple, true, age-sized answer to the question they actually asked, no more. Give an older child the fuller picture, including the parts that are harder and the parts the world will lie to them about. The conversation grows with the child, which is one more reason it cannot be a single talk. It is a relationship that stays open as the child changes.

## This week

Decide that you are the one who will talk about this, and then lower the stakes. You do not need a perfect speech. You need to be askable. The next time your child raises anything close to the subject, however awkwardly, answer plainly, calmly, and without ending the conversation. If nothing comes up naturally this week, find one small opening yourself, suited to their age, and prove to them with one ordinary conversation that this door is open. Then keep it open for the next ten years.

title: How to Parent a Strong-Willed Child
excerpt: The strong will that exhausts you at six may be the spine that saves your child at sixteen. The work is to shape it, not to break it.
body:
Every parent of a strong-willed child has been told, usually by someone whose children are compliant, that they simply need to be firmer. The advice misunderstands the child. A strong-willed child is not a discipline problem to be solved with more force. They are a person built with an unusually strong sense of self, and that strength is not your enemy. It is the very thing that, rightly shaped, will let them stand alone against a crowd one day. Your job is to bend it without breaking it.

This is some of the most tiring parenting there is. I am not writing from above it.

## Stop trying to win

The instinct with a defiant child is to win, to establish once and for all who is in charge. But a strong-willed child does not learn from being crushed. They learn that power is everything and that the lesson is to get stronger so they can win next time. You can dominate a toddler. You cannot dominate a teenager, and the years between will teach them whether your relationship runs on power or on trust.

Decide which hills are worth dying on, and there are fewer than you think. Safety, honesty, how we treat people. Those are non-negotiable. The color of the shirt, the order of the bedtime tasks, the hundred small preferences a child wants to control are places to hand over real choices. A strong-willed child who is given genuine authority over the small things fights you far less over the large ones.

## Offer choices inside firm walls

The strong will is a hunger for agency. Feed it on purpose. Instead of "put on your shoes," try "do you want the blue shoes or the black ones?" The boundary is fixed, shoes are happening, but the child gets to exercise the will that is straining for somewhere to go.

This is not manipulation. It is recognizing that God made this child with a strong sense of their own want, and training that want to operate inside limits rather than against them. You are not trying to erase the will. You are teaching it to live somewhere.

## Keep your own composure

A strong-willed child is an exquisite reader of your emotional state, and they will escalate to find the edge of it. The parent who loses control has handed the child a victory and a map. Proverbs says a person without self-control is like a city broken into, without walls. Your calm is the wall.

This means doing your own work. When you feel the heat rising, that is your signal to slow down, not speed up. "I am not going to argue about this. The answer is no. You can be upset about it." Said evenly, that holds. Said in a shout, it becomes a contest you may lose.

## See the gift inside the difficulty

It helps, on the hard days, to remember what this trait becomes. The strong will that refuses your bedtime is the same will that will refuse to cheat when everyone else does, refuse to follow the crowd into something cheap, refuse to abandon a conviction under pressure. Daniel had a strong will. So did the prophets. The world is changed by people who do not fold, and you are raising one.

Tell the child this, in words they can hold. "You have a strong heart. We are going to teach it to follow God, and then there is almost nothing it cannot do." A strong-willed child who believes their strength is a gift to be aimed grows up very differently than one who believes it is a flaw to be apologized for.

## Stay connected through the conflict

The danger with a strong-willed child is that the constant friction slowly erodes the relationship, until all that is left between you is the fighting. Guard against this on purpose. After a hard battle, reconnect. Find the things you genuinely enjoy together and protect them from the war. A strong-willed child needs to know that your love for them is not a casualty of the conflict, that you can be on opposite sides of a rule and still be deeply for them. The relationship is the bank account every limit draws from. Keep depositing into it, especially on the days the withdrawals are heavy, or you will find yourself one day with all rules and no relationship left to enforce them through.

## This week

Find one fight you have been having that does not actually matter, and hand the choice to your child. Watch what happens to the larger battles when the smaller one is theirs. Then, on a calm afternoon, tell your strong-willed child that their strong heart is something God gave them on purpose, and that you are going to help them aim it. Say it before the next storm, so they have it stored up when the storm comes.

title: How to Help an Anxious Child
excerpt: An anxious child does not need their fear erased or argued away. They need a steady adult to borrow calm from until they grow their own.
body:
When your child is anxious, every instinct in you wants to fix it, fast. You want to reassure the fear out of existence, to prove with logic that the monster is not real, to make the bad feeling stop because watching it is unbearable. Almost none of that works, and some of it makes things worse. An anxious child is not asking you to solve the problem. They are asking whether they are safe, and whether you can hold what they cannot.

This is gentle work, and it is slow. There is no sentence that ends anxiety. But there are ways of being with a frightened child that, over time, teach their nervous system that the world is more bearable than it feels.

## Do not argue with the fear

The reflex is to reason. "There is nothing to be scared of. That could never happen. You are being silly." To the anxious child, this lands as: you do not understand, and now I am also wrong for feeling this. Anxiety does not respond to argument because it does not come from the reasoning part of the mind. You cannot debate it into submission.

Instead, name it and stay near it. "That feels really scary right now. I am right here." You are not agreeing that the danger is real. You are agreeing that the fear is real, which it is, and a child whose fear is acknowledged settles faster than one whose fear is dismissed.

## Be the calm they borrow

Children regulate their emotions by borrowing yours first. A small child who falls looks at the parent's face to decide how hurt to be. The anxious child does the same with fear. If you meet their panic with panic, you have doubled it. If you meet it with steadiness, you have handed them something solid to hold.

This is hard, because an anxious child often has an anxious parent, and the fear in the room is partly yours. Do your own breathing first. Lower your voice. Slow your body down. You are not faking calm; you are choosing to go first into it, so they have a path to follow. "Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you," Peter writes. Part of how a child learns to cast their fear on God is by first casting it on a parent who does not flinch.

## Teach the body, not just the mind

Anxiety lives in the body, so help the body before you talk to the mind. Slow breathing, in through the nose, out long and slow, with you doing it alongside them. A hand on the chest to feel it settle. Naming five things they can see in the room. These are not tricks. They are ways of telling an alarmed nervous system that it is safe to stand down.

Do this when they are calm, too, not only mid-panic. A child who has practiced these in peace can reach for them in the storm. You are giving them tools they will carry into adulthood, long after they stop needing your hand.

## Hand the fear to God, honestly

The Christian answer to fear is not that fear is faithless and must be hidden. The Psalms are full of frightened people speaking their fear plainly to God. Teach your child to do the same. Pray with them, out loud, naming the actual fear. "God, the dark feels scary tonight. Please be near. Help us not be afraid."

Do not promise them that nothing bad will ever happen, because that is not a promise God makes and your child will eventually catch you in it. Promise them instead that they are not alone in it, that God is near the brokenhearted, and that you are not going anywhere. That is a promise you can keep.

## This week

The next time your child is anxious, resist the urge to argue the fear away. Name it, get your own body calm first, and breathe slowly alongside them until the wave passes. Then, on an ordinary calm evening, pray with them and let them speak their real fear out loud to God. You are teaching them, one settled moment at a time, that fear can be carried and that they do not have to carry it alone. If the anxiety is constant or growing, do not white-knuckle it; a wise counselor is a gift, not a failure.

title: How to Stay Close to a Teenager Who Is Pulling Away
excerpt: A teenager pulling away is doing exactly what they are supposed to do. The work is to stay reachable without chasing, present without smothering.
body:
There is a particular grief in watching a child who once told you everything become a teenager who answers in one syllable. You feel the door closing and you want to force it. But the pulling away is not a malfunction. It is the work of becoming a separate person, and a teenager who never pulls away has a different and worse problem. The goal is not to stop the separation. It is to stay close through it, so that when they come back, and they do come back, the relationship is still there.

This season humbled me. The parenting moves that worked when they were small stopped working overnight, and I had to learn new ones in the dark.

## Stop interrogating, start being available

The instinct when a teenager goes quiet is to ask more questions. "How was your day? What happened? Why won't you talk to me?" Every question feels to them like a demand, and they answer with the silence that demands earn. The harder you pursue, the faster they retreat.

Try the opposite. Be present without prying. Drive them somewhere and say nothing. Sit in the kitchen while they eat and talk about nothing important. Teenagers open up sideways, on their own schedule, usually in a car or late at night, and almost never when summoned. Your job is to be reliably around and unthreatening, so that when the moment comes, you are there to catch it. The conversations you want cannot be scheduled. They can only be made possible.

## Respect the door they are closing

A teenager building a separate self needs you to honor the boundary, not breach it. Knock on the closed door. Ask before reading the diary. Give them privacy that is real, not surveillance dressed as trust. Yes, you watch for genuine danger, and there are limits to privacy when safety is on the line. But the daily texture should be respect, because a teenager who feels respected stays connected, and one who feels spied on disappears.

This is the hardest pivot for a parent who used to know everything. You are moving from manager to consultant, from someone who runs their life to someone they might choose to ask. The authority you cling to, you lose. The trust you extend, you tend to get back.

## Stay warm even when they are cold

The teenager will test whether your love depends on their affection. They will be sullen, dismissive, sometimes cruel, and watch to see if you withdraw. Do not. Stay warm in the face of cold. Keep saying good morning to the grunt. Keep saying I love you to the eye roll. Keep showing up to the game even when they act like they did not want you there.

This is the love the father shows in the parable, the one who keeps the porch light on and the heart open while the son is far off. Your steadiness is the fixed point they push against to find their shape. They need you to not move. "Love is patient," Paul writes, and the teen years are where that sentence gets tested down to the bone.

## Keep doing things shoulder to shoulder

Teenagers who will not talk face to face will often talk side by side. Find something to do together that is not a conversation. Cook. Drive. Throw a ball. Work on the car. Watch their show, the one you do not understand, and let them explain it. Connection in these years comes through shared activity more than through talking about feelings. Get next to them doing something, and the words come on their own.

## Keep the door open with your own steadiness

More than anything, a teenager needs to know that the way back is always open, no matter how far they have wandered or how badly a conversation went. Do not close the door from your side in a moment of hurt or anger. They may slam it from theirs a hundred times. You hold yours open. When they say something cruel, do not retaliate in kind, even when you want to. When they push you away, do not stay away. The pulling away is a test of whether your love is sturdy enough to outlast their need to separate, and your steadiness across these years is the answer. They are watching, even when they pretend not to, to see whether you will still be there when the storm of adolescence passes. Be there. That is the whole assignment.

## This week

Pick one day and ask your teenager nothing. Instead, be present and easy, available without an agenda. Then find one shoulder-to-shoulder thing, however small, and do it with them. When they are cold, stay warm anyway. You are proving across this whole season that the door is open from your side and always will be, and that when they are ready to walk back through it, you will be exactly where they left you.

title: How to Answer Your Child's Hard Questions About God
excerpt: When your child asks a question you cannot answer, the answer they most need is not certainty. It is a parent who will not flinch and will not lie.
body:
Sooner or later your child will ask you something about God that you cannot answer, and how you respond in that moment will teach them more than the answer ever could. Why did grandma die? If God is real, why is there so much suffering? How do you know the Bible is true? Why does God let bad things happen to kids? These questions are not attacks on the faith. They are the faith, growing up, starting to feel the weight of the world.

The worst thing you can do is panic, shut it down, or fake a certainty you do not have. Children can smell a parent bluffing, and a faith that cannot survive a hard question is a faith they will leave the moment they meet a hard world.

## Welcome the question before you answer it

The first move is not the answer. It is the welcome. "That is a really good question." "I am glad you asked me that." You are teaching your child that doubt and hard questions are allowed in this house, that they can bring their honest confusion to you and to God without being shamed for it.

This matters enormously. Many people who left the faith did not leave over an argument. They left because the question they raised as a teenager was met with anger or fear, and they concluded the whole thing was too fragile to hold their real thoughts. Do not make the faith look brittle by guarding it nervously. A confident faith can sit with a hard question for a long time.

## Say "I don't know" when you don't

You will not have all the answers, and pretending you do is the fastest way to lose your credibility. When you do not know, say so. "I don't know. That is one of the hardest questions there is, and people much smarter than me have wrestled with it for thousands of years."

This does not weaken your witness. It strengthens it. You are showing your child that faith is not the absence of unanswered questions, that you can trust God without understanding everything, that honest is more durable than airtight. "I don't know, but here is what I do believe" is one of the most faith-building sentences a parent can say.

## Sit in the hard ones honestly

For the question of suffering, do not reach for a tidy answer, because there is not one and your child will know it. The Bible itself does not hand us a clean theory of pain. It hands us Job, who never gets his explanation, and a God who shows up in the whirlwind rather than in a syllogism. It hands us Jesus weeping at a tomb he was about to open.

So sit in it with your child. "I don't fully understand why God allows suffering. But I know he is not far from it. Jesus cried at his friend's grave. God came into the suffering himself, on the cross. He did not stay away from the pain." That is not a solved problem. It is a God in the room, which is what a hurting child actually needs.

## Point past yourself

You are not the source of your child's faith, and you cannot argue them into it. Your job is to be honest, to keep the door open, and to point them to God himself. When you do not have the answer, you can still say, "Let's ask God about it together," and pray the question out loud. You can still open the Bible and look together rather than lecturing.

The aim is not to win every conversation but to keep your child in the conversation, with you and with God, for the long haul. A child who learns they can bring anything to God will keep coming back to him long after they stop needing you to translate.

## This week

The next time your child asks something hard about God, do not rush to fix it. Welcome the question first, answer honestly, and if you do not know, say so and turn it into something you wrestle with together. If you want to be ready, the deep guide at /life/raising-children-in-grace sits with several of these questions at length. But readiness is not the point. Being a parent who does not flinch is the point. Let your child learn this week that there is no question too big to bring to you, and none too big to bring to God.

title: How to Apologize to Your Kids
excerpt: A parent who apologizes is not undermining their authority. They are teaching the one lesson about grace that no sermon can deliver.
body:
Many of us were raised by parents who never said they were sorry, who believed admitting fault would erode their authority, and so they doubled down on every mistake. We carry that instinct into our own parenting without examining it. But a parent who cannot apologize is not teaching strength. They are teaching their children that the powerful never have to repent, which is a lie about God and about how the world should work.

Learning to apologize to your children may be the most important repair work you do. It is also, for many of us, the hardest, because it means going first into the very humility we keep demanding from them.

## Why your apology matters more than you think

Your child will not learn what repentance looks like from a sermon. They will learn it from watching you. When you sin against your child, lose your temper, break a promise, accuse them of something they did not do, you have a choice. You can pretend it did not happen, justify it, or own it. Only one of those teaches the gospel.

A parent who apologizes shows a child several things at once: that wrongs can be named, that the relationship is bigger than the offense, that being wrong is survivable, and that love does not require pretending to be perfect. Confess your sins to one another, James writes. That includes confessing them to the small people in your house.

## Apologize fully, not halfway

The non-apology is worse than no apology, and children spot it instantly. "I'm sorry you got upset" is not an apology; it blames their reaction. "I'm sorry, but you made me angry" is not an apology; it is an accusation wearing a costume. A real apology owns the wrong without conditions.

A full apology has four parts. Name what you did: "I yelled at you, and that was wrong." Do not minimize or explain it away. Acknowledge the harm: "That probably scared you and hurt you, and you did not deserve it." Ask for forgiveness: "Will you forgive me?" That question hands real power to your child and means it. And commit to change: "I am going to work on my temper." Then actually work on it, because an apology you repeat weekly with no change becomes noise.

## Do not erase your authority by apologizing

Some parents fear that apologizing makes them weak, that the child will lose respect or use it against them later. The opposite happens. Children respect a parent who can own a wrong far more than one who never admits to any. Authority built on pretended perfection is brittle; the first obvious failure shatters it. Authority that can say sorry is durable, because it does not depend on the impossible. The respect you fear losing is the respect a real apology earns.

Apologizing for your sin does not mean apologizing for your standards. You can be sorry for how you said something and still hold the line you were defending. "I was right that you needed to stop, but I was wrong to scream it. I am sorry for the screaming." That sentence keeps the boundary and repairs the relationship at the same time. It models exactly the kind of person you are trying to raise.

## Let them see the whole cycle

The most powerful thing is for your child to see the entire arc: the failure, the conviction, the confession, the change. That is the shape of the Christian life, and they will live it ten thousand times. If they only ever see you fail, or only ever see you pretend not to, they learn a half-truth. When they see you fail, own it, and change, they learn that grace is not a doctrine but a way of living.

This is, in the end, you preaching the gospel with your own life. You are showing them a person who is forgiven, who knows it, and who therefore does not need to defend the illusion of being faultless. That is the freest thing you can model.

## This week

Think of one wrong you have done to your child that you have never owned, even a small one, even an old one. Go to them and apologize fully: name it, acknowledge the harm, ask forgiveness, and commit to change. Do not soften it with a "but." Then watch what it does, not just to them, but to you. You will find that going first into repentance in your own home is harder and more freeing than almost anything else you do as a parent.

title: How to Bless Your Children
excerpt: Your children are listening for one thing underneath everything else: whether you delight in them. Blessing is how you say it out loud, on purpose, again and again.
body:
There is an ancient practice nearly lost in modern parenting: the spoken blessing. Throughout Scripture, fathers laid hands on their children and spoke words over their lives. Jacob blessed his sons. Jesus took children in his arms and blessed them. The practice assumes something we have forgotten, that words spoken over a child have weight, that a parent's blessing leaves a mark, and that children are waiting, often their whole lives, to hear it.

Many adults are still listening for a word their father or mother never spoke. You can break that pattern. You can be the parent who says it.

## What a blessing actually is

A blessing is not flattery and not a performance review. It is a parent speaking, with intention, that this child is loved, seen, and delighted in, apart from anything they have achieved. It says: I am glad you exist. I see who you are. I am for you. God is for you.

The model is the Father's word over Jesus at his baptism: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." Notice the timing. This was spoken before Jesus had preached a sermon, healed anyone, or gone to the cross. The delight came first, before the work. That is the order a blessing follows. You delight in your child before they have earned it, because that is how God's love runs, and a child who receives love that way grows up able to give it.

## Touch, words, and a future

A full blessing has a few simple parts, drawn from the old patterns. There is meaningful touch, a hand on the shoulder, an arm around them, the child held while the words are spoken, because the body remembers what the ears might forget. There are spoken words of love and high value, said out loud and to their face. And there is a word picturing a good future, a parent's confidence that God has good things ahead for this child.

It can be as simple as this, at bedtime, hand on their head: "You are my son. I love you. I am proud of who you are becoming. God made you for good things, and I cannot wait to see them. The Lord bless you and keep you." That last line is Aaron's blessing from Numbers, spoken over Israel for three thousand years. You can speak it over your child tonight.

## Bless the being, not just the doing

Most of what children hear from us is about their doing. Good job, nice work, you did well, you did poorly. The blessing is different. It speaks to their being, to who they are rather than what they produced. A child fed only on praise for performance learns that love is earned and conditional, and they spend their lives auditioning. A child who is blessed for simply being theirs learns that love is given, which is the only soil a real life grows in.

So bless the things that are not achievements. Their kindness. Their courage. The particular way they see the world. The fact that they are yours. Tell them you would choose them again. This is the love that does not depend on the report card, and it is the love that holds when the report card is bad.

## Make it a rhythm

A blessing spoken once is a gift. A blessing spoken as a rhythm becomes the ground a child stands on. Build it into something that already happens, the way family worship attaches to a meal. Bless them at bedtime. Bless them as they leave for school. Bless them on birthdays with something longer and more particular. Let your children grow up so used to hearing that they are loved and delighted in that they could not point to the day it started, only know it was always true.

The family devotions and seasonal resources at /family/devotions can help you build this into the year. But the words are yours to say, and your voice is the one your child is listening for.

## This week

Tonight, put a hand on your child and say a blessing out loud. Keep it simple: I love you, I am glad you are mine, I see who you are becoming, God has good things for you. Use Aaron's words if you have none of your own. Then do it again tomorrow, and the night after, until it becomes the thing your child knows without remembering when they learned it. You are answering, in advance, the question they will carry their whole lives: am I delighted in? Make sure the answer is yes, and make sure they heard it from you.

title: How to Raise Kids Who Own Their Faith
excerpt: You cannot hand your child a faith they merely inherit. You can only raise them in conditions where a faith of their own has room to grow.
body:
Every Christian parent fears the same thing: that their child will walk away from the faith. The fear drives some parents to control, to tighten the rules and shrink the questions, believing that a faith held firmly enough by the parent will transfer to the child. It almost never works that way. A faith that is only inherited, never owned, tends to fall off the first time the world pushes hard. The children who keep their faith are usually the ones who were allowed to make it theirs.

You cannot save your child. You were never able to. What you can do is tend the soil, and trust the One who actually grows things.

## Faith caught more than taught

Children absorb the faith you live far more than the faith you explain. They watch whether your religion makes you kinder or harsher, whether you pray when no one is looking, whether grace is something you preach or something you practice on them at the kitchen table. A faith that is real in the ordinary fabric of the home is contagious. A faith that is performed on Sunday and absent on Tuesday teaches them that the whole thing is theater.

This is humbling, because it means the most important curriculum is your own life. Paul could tell the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitated Christ. The question for us is narrower and harder: if my child imitates the faith they actually see in me, where will it take them? That question should shape us before it shapes them.

## Make room for doubt

The parents whose children most often keep the faith are frequently the ones who let their children question it. This feels backward, but it holds. A faith that was never allowed to be questioned was never really owned; it was only borrowed, and borrowed things get returned. When you welcome your child's doubts instead of fearing them, you teach that the faith is sturdy enough to be examined, and that they do not have to choose between honesty and belief.

So when the hard questions come, and they will, do not shut them down. Welcome them. "That is a good question, let's think about it." A child who can bring their doubt to you will keep bringing it, and a doubt brought into the light tends to resolve toward faith far more often than one driven into hiding. The deep guide at /life/raising-children-in-grace and the piece on answering hard questions go further into this. The short version: do not be afraid of their questions. Be afraid of their silence.

## Let it cost something

A faith that costs nothing is worth nothing, and children sense this. If following Jesus in your home means only comfort, never sacrifice, your child learns that faith is a consumer good. But if they see the faith cost you something, generosity that pinches, forgiveness that is hard, honesty when a lie would be easier, telling the truth when it is expensive, they learn that this is real, because real things cost.

Give them ways to live it out, not just believe it. Serve someone together. Give until it is felt. Let them see you choose the harder right over the easier wrong and name why. Faith becomes their own when they have spent something on it. James said faith without works is dead, and a child raised on belief without action is being handed a corpse.

## Aim for relationship, not behavior

It is possible to raise a child who keeps all the rules and knows nothing of God, and many of us have done exactly that without meaning to. If the goal becomes managing behavior, you can produce a moral child with a dead heart, which is the Pharisee's trajectory. The goal is not a well-behaved child. It is a child who knows God, who has met him personally, who prays not to satisfy you but because they have found Someone worth talking to.

So keep pointing past yourself and past the rules to God himself. Pray with them in ways that are real. Read the Bible as a place to meet a Person, not a rulebook to memorize. Tell them what God has done in your own life, including recently, including the hard parts. You are introducing them to Someone, and an introduction is not the same as enforcement.

## This week

Do one thing that lets your child's faith become theirs rather than yours. Welcome a doubt instead of fearing it. Let them see the faith cost you something real and tell them why you paid it. Pray with them in a way that is honest rather than rote. And then loosen your grip, because the thing you are most afraid of is not finally in your hands. Tend the soil this week, and trust the One who grows things to do what you cannot.

title: How to Lead Your Family When You Feel Like a Failure
excerpt: The qualification to lead your family was never your competence. It is your willingness to keep showing up, repenting, and pointing past yourself to God.
body:
Most parents, at some point, lie awake convinced they are failing their children. The temper they cannot fix. The patience they do not have. The faith they preach but do not feel. The sense that everyone else has this figured out and they alone are unfit for the people sleeping down the hall. If that is you, read this slowly. You are not disqualified. You may, in fact, be closer to the truth than the parents who feel sure of themselves.

The Bible is not a record of competent leaders. It is a record of God using broken ones who kept turning back to him.

## God has always led through failures

Look at who God put in charge. Abraham lied about his wife to save his own skin, twice. Jacob deceived his father and played favorites with his sons, and the damage rippled for generations. David, called a man after God's own heart, was a catastrophe of a father. Moses argued that he was the wrong man for the job and was right about most of his weaknesses. God led his people through every one of them.

The pattern is unmistakable, and it should loosen something in your chest. God does not wait for qualified parents because there are none. He uses the parent who keeps coming back to him over the parent who has it all together, because the second kind does not exist and the first kind is teachable. Your sense of inadequacy is not evidence you should quit. It may be the very thing that keeps you on your knees, which is exactly where a parent belongs.

## Repentance is the leadership

You will fail your children. The question is never whether, only what you do next. And here is the thing the competent-looking parents often miss: your repentance is not the interruption of your leadership. It is the leadership. When your children watch you fail, own it, turn back to God, and try again, they are learning the single most important thing you can teach them, which is what to do with their own failure.

A family does not need a flawless leader. It needs a leader who knows where to turn when they are not flawless. Lead from weakness, out loud. Let them see you ask God for help you clearly need. Paul learned that God's power is made perfect in weakness, and that he would rather boast in his weakness so that power could rest on him. That is not a consolation prize for failures. That is the actual mechanism. The cracked vessel is the one the light gets through.

## Show up tomorrow

Most of parenting is not won in great moments but in the refusal to quit after bad ones. You yelled tonight. You were absent this week. You said the wrong thing. None of that is final unless you let it become final by giving up. The single most powerful thing a struggling parent can do is show up again tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after that.

Faithfulness over time covers a multitude of individual failures. The parent who is present and repentant across ten thousand ordinary days, most of them imperfect, is doing something a single spectacular failure cannot undo. Lamentations says God's mercies are new every morning. So is your chance to parent. You do not have to fix everything. You have to get up.

## Point past yourself

Here is the deepest relief, and the heart of it. You were never your children's savior. You cannot be, and the attempt to be is itself a kind of pride wearing the mask of love. There is already a Savior, and it is not you. Your job is not to be perfect for your children. It is to point them, with your imperfect life, to the One who is.

This frees you from a burden you were never meant to carry. You can stop pretending to be enough and start showing your children where real enough is found. The most honest thing you can say to your child is also the most freeing thing you can say to yourself: I get it wrong a lot, and there is Someone who never does, and we are both running to him together.

## This week

If you are carrying the weight of feeling like a failure, do two things this week. First, repent out loud where your children can see it, not as a show but as the lesson it actually is, so they learn what to do with their own failures by watching you handle yours. Second, get up tomorrow and show up again, imperfect, undeterred, present. You do not have to save your children. You only have to keep pointing them to the One who can, and keep walking that road yourself, one ordinary day at a time.
